764.title: Ali in the bed
764.hook: Ali sleeps in the Prophet's bed, and stays to return the Meccans' deposits (sirah)
764.howItsDone: Muslims retell Ali's night in the Prophet's bed as part of the hijra story, and point to the returned deposits when they speak of amana, keeping what is entrusted to you.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the plot in the council house. Your line was: they planned; Allah planned.

Night. Outside the house of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, young men from every clan are waiting with their swords, watching the door. Ibn Ishaq says they planned to strike when he came out. Inside, the Prophet turns to his young cousin, Ali, and gives him a strange instruction. Lie down on my bed. Wrap yourself in my green cloak and sleep in it. Nothing you dislike will happen to you. Today: Ali in the bed.
screen: `SWORDS AT THE DOOR.` → `LIE DOWN ON MY BED.` → `WRAP YOURSELF IN MY CLOAK.`

segments.voice: So Ali lies down where the men outside expect their target to be. Through the night they see a shape under the Prophet's cloak, and they wait. Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet went out among them, took a handful of dust, and scattered it over their heads, reciting from Ya Sin: and We have covered them so that they see not. He passed, and they didn't see him. In the morning someone tells them he's gone. They look at the bed again, and it's Ali who gets up. But Ali's job isn't finished. Ibn Ishaq says that people in Mecca who had something they feared for left it with the Prophet, because he was known for his honesty. Tradition calls him al-Amin, the trustworthy. When he left, Ibn Ishaq says, he told Ali to stay behind and return every one of those deposits to its owners. And Ali did. For days, in a city that had just tried to kill his cousin, he went door to door handing back what belonged to them. Then he set out for Yathrib himself. Some of the people who had left those deposits were the same people who wanted him dead. And the Prophet's instruction about them, on the night he ran for his life, was about their property: make sure they get it back. Trust held, even toward them.

segments.voice: Take a slow inventory of what you're holding that isn't yours: a borrowed book, a dish from someone's kitchen, money you owe, a favor promised, even somebody's secret, which is also held in trust. Let each one come to mind without guilt, just as a list, and picture handing one of them back. If you pray, you can ask God to help you keep what's entrusted to you.
Al-Amin, the trustworthy: what Mecca called the Prophet, the reason people left their valuables with him even the night men waited outside his door with swords. Today's word.
Your line: trusts returned, even then. Ali's job wasn't glamorous: knock, hand it back, next door. That's today's lesson.

765.title: "The dearest land"
765.hook: leaving, he says to Mecca: you are the dearest land to me, and if your people hadn't driven me out I'd never have left (Tirmidhi)
765.howItsDone: Many Muslims quote the Prophet's farewell to Mecca when they speak of love for one's homeland, and Mecca remains the city Muslims face in prayer and travel to on pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Amin, and Ali returning every trust. Your line was: trusts returned, even then.

The city that just tried to kill him is behind him now. Its leaders mocked him. Its council voted on his death. Its young men waited at his door with swords. And as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, leaves it, the hadith keep words he speaks to it. Not to the people. To the place itself. Two companions report what he said, and both reports are kept in the collection of al-Tirmidhi. Today: Mecca.
screen: `THE CITY BEHIND HIM.` → `HE SPEAKS TO MECCA.` → `HE SPEAKS TO THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: In one report, from Abdullah ibn Adi, the Prophet stands at a spot in Mecca and says: by God, you are the best of God's earth, and the dearest of God's earth to God. And if I had not been driven out of you, I would never have left. In the other, from Ibn Abbas, he speaks more personally: how good you are as a land, and how dear you are to me. If my people had not driven me out, I would never have lived anywhere but you. Listen to the two halves. The first is pure love: dearest, best, how good you are. The second names what happened, with no softening: I was driven out. He doesn't pretend he's leaving by choice. And he doesn't let what the people did turn into hatred for the place. The Qur'an uses the same plain language: the town that drove you out. Grief and love, and the truth about why, all in two sentences. Anyone who has left a hometown, a country, a house they grew up in, may know the shape of it. You can love a place and still be forced to leave it, and you can say both out loud. Mecca will come back into his life later. Here, he says goodbye.
screen: `THE DEAREST OF GOD'S EARTH.` · `IF I HADN'T BEEN DRIVEN OUT.` · `LOVE AND TRUTH TOGETHER.` · `THE TOWN THAT DROVE YOU OUT.` · then, large: `THE DEAREST LAND.`

segments.voice: Let a place you've left come to you, a childhood home, a city, a room that isn't yours anymore, and walk through it slowly: the light, the smell, who was there. If the reason you left still stings, let it be true without arguing with it, then silently tell the place what it was to you, in one or two plain sentences, the way he did. If you pray, you can thank God for that place.
Mecca. Leaving the city, the Prophet told it he would never have left if he hadn't been driven out, the dearest land to him. Today's word.
Your line: grief and love, both true. Neither one had to cancel the other. See you tomorrow.

766.title: The cave of Thawr
766.hook: three nights hidden in a cave, the searchers at its mouth, and the verse: Allah is with us (9:40)
766.howItsDone: Muslims recite 9:40 and retell the cave of Thawr when they remember the hijra, and Abu Bakr is remembered as the companion in the cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mecca, and his farewell to the dearest land. Your line was: grief and love, both true.

Footsteps on rock, just overhead. Voices. Men from Quraysh have tracked the fugitives up a mountain outside Mecca, and now they're standing at the mouth of a cave, close enough that the two men hiding inside can see their feet. In the dark are the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr, his companion on the road out of Mecca. Neither of them moves. Neither of them breathes too loudly. Today: Thawr.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS OVERHEAD.` → `FEET AT THE MOUTH OF THE CAVE.` → `TWO MEN IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr remembers the moment himself. He whispers: if one of them looks down at his feet, he'll see us. And the Prophet answers: what do you think, Abu Bakr, of two when God is their third? One frightened sentence, one quiet question back. The Qur'an remembers the same night. In Pickthall's translation, it speaks of when the two were in the cave, and he said to his companion: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." And God, the verse goes on, sent down His peace upon him. Neither text has an escape plan, or a promise that the searchers will leave. Just: we are not two. The searchers do leave. And Bukhari's longer account, from Aisha, shows how the hiding worked. They stayed in the cave three nights. Abu Bakr's son Abdullah, a sharp young man, spent the nights with them and slipped back into Mecca before dawn, so that by day he was in the city like anyone else, listening for every plot against them, and brought the news back after dark. A freed servant of Abu Bakr's, Amir ibn Fuhayra, grazed sheep nearby, brought them milk in the evening, and moved on again before dawn. So faith in the story isn't the opposite of planning. The planning is careful. It's the fear that gets answered, not with a plan, but with a question: two, and God the third.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or cover them with your hands, and let the dark be what it is; notice your breath, and whatever worry is nearest, the way footsteps were nearest for Abu Bakr. If you pray, you can say the line from the verse: Allah is with us.

767.title: Asma's belt
767.hook: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma tears her waistband in two to tie the food bags, and is called she of the two belts (Bukhari)
767.howItsDone: Muslims retell Asma bint Abi Bakr's part in the hijrah from Sahih al-Bukhari and know her by the name it gave her: dhat al-nitaqayn, she of the two belts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Thawr, two men hidden in the dark with searchers at the mouth. Your line was: two, and Allah the third.

A food bag, a water skin, and no string. That's the whole problem in today's story, and it happens in a house in Mecca on the night two men are about to vanish. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr are leaving for Yathrib in secret. Somebody has to pack the food. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr's daughter, Asma, tells us what happened in that kitchen. The meal is ready. The bags are ready. And there's nothing in the house to tie them shut. Today: Asma's belt.
screen: `NO STRING.` → `A SECRET NIGHT.` → `ASMA IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene as Asma tells it. She prepared the journey food for the Prophet and her father. They looked for something to bind the food bag and the water skin, and found nothing. So she said to her father, in effect: by Allah, I can find nothing to tie it with except my waistband. And Abu Bakr answered: then tear it in two. Tie the water skin with one half and the food with the other. She did. And from that night on, she says, she was called dhat al-nitaqayn: she of the two belts. No miracle, no clever plan. A young woman uses the cloth already wrapped around her, and the great journey of the hijrah leaves the house tied shut with half of a waistband. Notice where she's standing, too. The men will be hidden in a cave. Asma is the one still in the city, in the house the searchers will come to. The sirah tells of her carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed, so her part wasn't finished in the kitchen. And her name doesn't remember a speech or a battle. It remembers a quick, practical choice made with what was in reach. Aisha's telling of the night, also in Bukhari, puts it a little differently: Asma cuts a piece of her belt rather than tearing it in two. Both keep the same picture: the bag closed with her own cloth. The road to Medina didn't begin with what anyone wished they had. It began with what was there.

If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with what is already in your hands.

768.title: Suraqa's horse
768.hook: Suraqa, chasing for the reward, sinks in the sand and turns back (Bukhari)
768.howItsDone: Muslims retell Suraqa ibn Malik's chase from his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the hijrah story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asma tore her waistband to tie the food bags. Your line was: two belts.

A price on two heads. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Suraqa ibn Malik tells this story himself. Messengers from Quraysh came to his tribe, offering a reward to anyone who killed or captured the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or Abu Bakr. Suraqa was sitting with his people when a man walked up: I just saw figures moving along the coast. I think it's them. Suraqa knew it was. And he said out loud: no, that's just some travelers we know. He wanted the reward for himself. Today: Suraqa's horse.
screen: `A PRICE ON TWO HEADS.` → `FIGURES ON THE COAST.` → `NO, JUST SOME TRAVELERS.`

segments.voice: He waits a little, goes home, and quietly sends his horse out behind a hill. He takes his spear and rides. As he nears them, his horse stumbles and throws him. In his own telling, he draws lots with divining arrows, the custom of the time, and the answer comes out against him: don't harm them. He rides anyway, close enough, he says, to hear the Prophet reciting. He notices the Prophet doesn't look back, while Abu Bakr keeps turning around to look. Then the ground gives way. His horse's forelegs sink into the earth up to the knees, and he's thrown. He urges the horse up; it can barely pull its legs out, and when it stands, dust rises from the tracks of its legs like smoke. He draws lots again, and again the answer is the one he doesn't want. At last Suraqa does what a hunter doesn't do. He calls out to the men he's chasing and asks for safety. They stop. He tells them everything: the reward, what people are planning. He offers them food and supplies. They take nothing. They ask only, in effect: keep our matter hidden. He asks for a written promise of safety, and Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr's freed man, writes it for him on a piece of leather. The fugitives never run faster. The chaser is the one who's stopped, by the ground and by his own lots, until he gives up the chase himself. The man who set out to sell them ends up guarding their secret, holding their promise in his hand.

769.title: Umm Ma'bad's goat
769.hook: the sirah tells of a thin goat in a woman's tent giving milk when he touched it
769.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Umm Ma'bad from the sirah literature, and her description of the Prophet's appearance is kept with the report.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suraqa, riding after the reward until his horse sank. Your line was: the sand held him back.

Dust, heat, and a tent on the road north. The travelers are hungry. They stop at the tent of a woman the sirah calls Umm Ma'bad, known for giving food and water to people passing by. They ask if she has meat or dates to sell. She has nothing. It's been a hard, dry season, and the flock is out grazing. All that's left at the tent is one goat, too thin and weak to go out with the others. This story isn't from Bukhari or Muslim; it comes from the sirah and other collections. Today: Umm Ma'bad.
screen: `A TENT ON THE ROAD.` → `NOTHING TO SELL.` → `ONE THIN GOAT.`

segments.voice: In the story, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, notices the goat at the side of the tent and asks Umm Ma'bad about it. Too weak to go with the flock, she says. Does the goat have any milk? Far too worn out for that. He asks her permission to milk her anyway, and her answer is lovely: if you see milk in her, then milk her. He rubs the goat's udder, says the name of Allah, and prays, and the milk comes. He calls for a vessel. Umm Ma'bad drinks first, then his companions, and he drinks last. He milks again and leaves the vessel full for her. Then they ride on. See who drinks first: the host, who had nothing to give. The guest who brought the milk drinks last. Later her husband, Abu Ma'bad, comes home driving the thin flock and sees the full vessel. Where did this come from? She describes the man who stopped by, his face, his eyes, his voice, and her description is kept with the story. A woman with nothing to offer becomes a witness. The story doesn't send her a feast. It takes the one weak thing at the edge of the tent, the goat everyone had given up on, and draws enough from it for everyone. Tomorrow the travelers reach the edge of Yathrib.

770.title: Quba and the first Friday
770.hook: at Quba he builds a mosque and leads the first Friday prayer on the way into the city (sirah)
770.howItsDone: Muslims gather each Friday at midday for Jumu'ah, a congregational prayer with a sermon (khutbah); visitors to Medina also pray at the mosque of Quba.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Ma'bad's thin goat. Your line was: from the dry goat, milk. This week: trusts returned, the dearest land, the cave, the belt, the horse, the goat.

For a while, people in Yathrib had walked out to the edge of town every morning to watch the road. That detail is in Bukhari. They'd heard he had left Mecca, so they waited, until the heat drove them back inside. One day a man up on a high place saw white-clad riders coming out of the shimmer and shouted the news. People ran out to meet them. The travelers didn't go straight into the city. They stopped first at Quba, a village on its outskirts. Today: al-jumu'ah.
screen: `WATCHING THE ROAD EACH MORNING.` → `RIDERS IN THE SHIMMER.` → `FIRST STOP, QUBA.`

segments.voice: In Bukhari's account, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stays some nights at Quba with the clan of Banu Amr ibn Awf, and lays the foundation of a mosque. Bukhari connects it to a verse in surah nine about a place of worship founded on devotion to Allah from its first day, with people in it who love to purify themselves. Muslims still pray at Quba today. Before a house for himself in the city, he builds a place to pray. Then he rides on toward the town. Ibn Ishaq says a Friday came while he was on the way, among the clan of Banu Salim ibn Awf, and he led the Friday prayer there, in a valley, with the people around him, the first he led in Medina. Some reports say the believers of Yathrib had already been gathering on Fridays before he came, so the careful way to say it is: his first Friday among them. Here's how the Qur'an names the day, in surah sixty-two, in Pickthall's words: "When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." The day of congregation. In Arabic, al-jumu'ah, the gathering. That's what this week has been walking toward. People slipping out of Mecca one by one, two men in a cave, a belt torn in half, a hunter turned back, a woman's thin goat. Scattered people on separate roads. And near the end of the road, before he has even entered the city, they gather, in a valley, on a Friday, and pray together.
